absent: Group setup, hierarchy lookup, and old-root connection algorithms beyond call sites and branching conditions.
Timer queue ordering, deadline propagation, migrator election, and wakeup handling.
Meaning and valid values of presence masks, migration state word, and capacity accounting.
Hotplug online and offline transition effects beyond callback registration names.
Timekeeper lock mechanics, VDSO write-section ordering, and arch synchronization effects.
Allocation layout and lifetime of hierarchy, group, and CPU-set objects.
Error codes from delegated activation and from setup beyond generic failure propagation.

findings.text: Hierarchy descriptor groups membership and level bookkeeping: a CPU set pointer, a current root pointer, a capacity count, a global linkage node, and a trailing flexible array of per-level list heads.
Migration event record combines a timer queue node for the next deadline with an owner CPU number and a disregard flag.

Group descriptor combines mutual exclusion, an upward link, an embedded group deadline event, a cached expiry instant, a head of member events, an atomic migration word, depth and node placement, a child count, a compact child presence mask, and list linkage.
Per-CPU descriptor combines mutual exclusion, availability plus idle plus remote flags, an assigned group link, a compact mask, a wakeup instant, and an embedded CPU deadline event.
Migration state can be observed as one 32-bit word or as a packed view splitting active indication, migrator indication, and sequence count.
Hierarchy fanout factor is eight children per group.
Header uses a single include guard macro to make double inclusion a no-op.

Addition of a CPU holds a global mutex for the entire lookup plus setup plus possible root linkage, and holds an additional migration guard while choosing and performing old-root linkage after a root change.
Per-CPU mutual exclusion is initialized during first prepare before the CPU is attached; both per-CPU and group descriptors each carry their own raw spin protection for later use.

Publication of time data for user mappings is bracketed by an IRQ-saving timekeeper lock: acquisition plus write-section open on begin, write-section close plus arch synchronization plus release with saved flags on end.
Startup requires the fanout factor to be a power of two at build time and returns immediate success without allocating or registering anything on a single-processor build.

On multiprocessor builds the depth is estimated from possible node and CPU counts under an even-spread assumption, separating node-local depth from cross-node depth and remembering the boundary where node matching is no longer needed.

Prepare succeeds immediately when the CPU already has an assigned group; otherwise it initializes locking, an empty queue at far-future deadline, disregard set, owner set, remote cleared, and far-future wakeup, then attaches and rejects a zero presence mask as invalid.
The hierarchy CPU set gains the new CPU only when setup and any required old-root linkage both succeed; lookup or setup errors propagate without changing membership.

Old-root handling after a root change has three mutually exclusive paths: local active propagation when the caller belongs to the hierarchy, delegated activation from another available CPU of that hierarchy when the caller is outside it, and remote linkage without propagation when that hierarchy has no available CPU.

Boot initialization allocates the available set, computes and logs depth configuration, then registers a prepare callback and an online pair for hotplug, failing with an error message if allocation or registration fails.
Time-data publication exposes a begin operation returning saved interrupt flags and an end operation taking those flags, with the write section and arch synchronization strictly nested between them.

Remote linkage without propagation leaves the old root inactive until some later activation; delegated activation can fail with the delegate error; a zero presence mask after apparently successful attachment indicates inconsistent hierarchy construction.
